claims.text: The naturally formed oxide film governs the corrosion resistance of pre-exposed Q235 steel in chloride-rich environments.
Elevated-temperature exposure alters the morphology of the native oxide film on Q235 steel relative to room-temperature exposure.
Thermal stresses can induce microcracking in the native oxide film on Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature can enhance diffusion of minor alloying elements such as Mn into or through the oxide film.
Temperature-induced changes in oxide morphology or composition modify the film's barrier properties.
Pre-exposed Q235 steel bears a thin, heterogeneous native oxide film.
A chloride-rich medium is an applicable environment for studying corrosion resistance of a Q235-based specimen.
At room temperature, an intact native oxide film passivates Q235 steel against chloride attack.
Thermal microcracking would reduce the protective integrity of the native oxide film.
Enrichment by diffusing alloying elements could increase oxide-film density and improve passivation.
Changes in oxide-film structure alter the diffusion barrier encountered by corrosive species.
Elevated-temperature samples will have measurably different oxide-film morphology or composition than room-temperature samples.
Elevated-temperature samples will have a corrosion rate different from that of the room-temperature reference.
The sign and magnitude of the corrosion-rate change depend on competition between film breakdown and possible film densification.
The proposed scope is Q235 steel with a native oxide layer in moderately aggressive chloride environments and service-relevant temperature ranges.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to steels with additional protective coatings or where other degradation mechanisms dominate.
A lack of statistically significant temperature-dependent differences in both oxide-film structure and corrosion rate would falsify the proposed temperature-driven oxide-film mechanism.
